gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a plug-in inverter's current never passes through the branch breaker. UL's wording is that 'the combined current from the utility and PIPV source can exceed conductor ratings without tripping the circuit breaker.' APsystems' own consumer page still says two EZ1s give 'up to 1,800W of plug-in solar power on a standard 15A circuit'. That is about 15 A the breaker cannot see, while the EZ1-LV's UL 3700 certificate conditions allow only a dedicated 10 A circuit.
standout_why: I compared five pages. solarunitedneighbors.org (cited) says only in general terms that generation 'can mask or hide the overloaded wiring', with no figures or products. pluginsolarcheck.com/kits/certifications (cited) and solarwaypoint.com (cited) report the EZ1-LV certificate condition ('dedicated 10 A circuit, or a listed bidirectional Class A GFCI on a non-dedicated circuit'), but they don't explain why it exists or put a number on the unseen current. None of them notes that APsystems' own consumer page advertises 1,800 W on a standard 15 A circuit, which goes against that condition. balconysolarkits.us (cited) doesn't cover circuit behaviour at all. SUN gives 160 ms as a deadline to stop exporting during an outage, but no page names a product that meets a plug de-energising time, which Hoymiles states for its plug.
decides: ChatGPT's 'best overall', the APsystems EZ1-LV (900 VA, about 7.5 A at 120 V), works only if the shopper has or adds a dedicated 10 A circuit, or a bidirectional GFCI on a shared circuit. Pairing two on one ordinary 15 A circuit, as APsystems' video copy suggests, means about 15 A the breaker cannot see, up to roughly 30 A worst case on 15 A wiring. A shopper with only shared outlets should start with a smaller Hoymiles HiFlow Pro LV (360–500 VA, about 3.0–4.17 A), which adds far less current the breaker can't see. Hoymiles also states its plug drops below 15 Vac within 0.16 s of being unplugged. The EZ1-LV is still the pick for a two-panel system on a dedicated circuit.

findings.label: Why a plug-in inverter can overload a branch circuit (UL's wording)
findings.value: "the combined current from the utility and PIPV source can exceed conductor ratings without tripping the circuit breaker"
findings.source_title: Safety Considerations for Plug-In Photovoltaic (PIPV) Systems | UL Solutions
findings.note: The breaker measures only current coming from the panel. Inverter current enters at the outlet and goes to loads on the same circuit without passing through the breaker. The page shows no byline or date, only © 2026 UL LLC.

findings.label: Fixes UL lists for the backfeed and live-plug hazards
findings.value: "Dedicated circuits with unique receptacles to prevent overloads"; "Bidirectional GFCI devices to maintain shock protection under backfeed conditions"; "Integrated overcurrent protection at the point of connection"; hazard: "Accessible plug blades can become energized when exposed to sunlight"
findings.source_title: Safety Considerations for Plug-In Photovoltaic (PIPV) Systems | UL Solutions

findings.label: Maker's claim for two units on one ordinary circuit
findings.value: "Two EZ1 units can even be paired together for up to 1,800W of plug-in solar power on a standard 15A circuit."
findings.note: From the description of the training video 'EZ1 Makes Balcony Solar Easy: 4-Panel Plug-In Installation Training' on APsystems' own page. Body text on the same page says it 'plugs directly into a standard wall outlet'. Arithmetic: 1,800 W / 120 V = 15 A of backfeed. Using UL's explanation, the worst case on a 15 A circuit is a segment of wire carrying 15 A from the panel plus 15 A from the inverters, about 30 A, before the breaker trips.

findings.label: Outage behaviour
findings.value: Shuts down during a grid outage and "Restarts only after grid power has been stable for five minutes"
findings.note: Page also says 'CSA certified to UL 3700 and meets UL 1741 SB requirements.' It gives no time for how fast the plug prongs lose power after unplugging.
